extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and performing short stand-up jokes (setups, punchlines, tags, callbacks) optimized for a 6-minute open-mic slot. Focuses on structural mechanics beginners should master before experimenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup + Punchline (core pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every joke has two parts: the setup plants an assumption in the audience's head; the punchline breaks that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Setup: 'My mom called me at 11 PM last night.' Punchline: 'To ask if I'd eaten dinner.' The setup makes you expect something serious; the punchline reveals something mundane. This mismatch is the mechanism of comedy. Everything else is decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag (second laugh)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tag is a smaller joke stacked on top of the main punchline — same premise, new angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sequence: Punchline: 'To ask if I'd eaten dinner.' Tag 1: 'I said yes. She then asked what I ate.' Tag 2: 'She then told me what I should have eaten.' Tags separate a beginner set from a tight one; one solid joke with two tags is worth three okay jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag count guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How many tags should you use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2-3 tags is strong. 4+ and you are beating a dead horse — audience stops laughing because they sense you are trying too hard on one premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 3
rubrics_metrics.description: List two normal things, then a third unexpected one; the first two lull the audience, the third breaks the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I moved to Mumbai for three things — the job, the energy, and the knowledge that I would never be able to afford a 2BHK.' Almost every comedian uses this. Use it because it works, but don't overuse it — not more than 2-3 times in a 6-minute set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback
rubrics_metrics.description: A callback references an earlier joke later in your set to reward audience attention and create a second laugh from one premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Open with a joke about your mom's intense wedding prep; 4 minutes later, reference that earlier joke during a different premise to get a 'free' laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage testing / perform live
rubrics_metrics.description: Every joke needs a stage to prove it works; stage time compounds and each mic makes the next easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book a 6-minute open-mic slot to test and refine jokes. Live performance reveals what lands and what needs rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline placement (avoid burying the punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The funniest word of your joke should be as close to the end as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak: 'I once saw an auto driver arguing about 5 rupees on the meter at 2 AM.' Strong: 'At 2 AM last week, an auto driver argued with me for twenty minutes. Over 5 rupees.' Tighter structure places the funny word at the end where the laugh belongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep setups short (avoid too many setups)
rubrics_metrics.description: One short setup, one punchline; beginners often pile multiple setups before a punchline which loses audience attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut ruthlessly; the setup should be as short as possible while still planting the assumption. One sentence is ideal, two is okay, three is usually too many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't explain the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: If the audience does not laugh, do not add clarifying words to explain the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining kills the joke and signals insecurity. Either trust the line or rewrite it so it lands without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut unnecessary words before the punchline (the one rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every unnecessary word before the punchline is dead weight; remove anything that isn't serving the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut until the joke hurts to cut any more — that is when it is stage-ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-liner definition and use
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-liner is a complete joke in a single sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harder to write, easier to forget, great for openers. Not required for beginners. Examples include Mitch Hedberg and Anuvab Pal one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to test if your joke structure is tight
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical test to evaluate tightness of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the joke aloud and underline every word you could remove without losing the joke. If you find 3+ removable words, the structure is loose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing process: punchline-first
rubrics_metrics.description: Most working comics write the punchline idea first and build the setup backwards from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The setup exists to serve the punchline, not the other way round. Start with the funny beat and craft the shortest setup that leads to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple punchlines (tag jokes) constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke can have multiple punchlines (tags), but the set should have one dominant laugh per premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only one punchline should be the biggest laugh; the others should feel like bonuses, not competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-thumb frequency limits for devices in a 6-minute set
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical limits on repeating structural devices within a short set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the rule of 3 more than 2-3 times in a 6-minute set. Likewise, avoid over-tagging one premise (4+ tags is too many). The 6-minute slot shapes how often you reuse devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-mic slot length (practical constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Buddy On Stage open-mic slots are 6 minutes long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 6-minute constraint to decide how many premises, tags, callbacks, and uses of structural devices you can realistically fit and polish.
